article_title: The longitudinal association between engagement and achievement varies by time, students’ profiles, and achievement state: A full program study
citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, Satu Helske, Stefan Hrastinski. (2023). The longitudinal association between engagement and achievement varies by time, students' profiles, and achievement state: A full program study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104787
title: Multi-channel sequence analysis with mixture hidden Markov models for longitudinal engagement-achievement trajectories
description: The article offers a detailed methodology for studying how engagement and achievement evolve together across a full program: two chronologically ordered state sequences (engagement and achievement channels) are aligned per course, and a Mixture Hidden Markov Model — "a combination of LCA and HMM" — clusters multichannel trajectories jointly while estimating transition probabilities between hidden states. The method models "several variables evolving in parallel" and reveals for whom and when engagement-achievement relations change across a program.
requirements: Multi-channel longitudinal data with chronologically ordered, synchronized state sequences per channel (e.g., LMS indicators per course plus course grades)
Model selection and estimation repeated with many random starting values; the article estimated MHMMs with varying hidden states and clusters, repeated 1000 times, selecting by BIC
constraints: Online trace data can only capture behavioral and cognitive engagement; the article does not explicitly operationalize emotional engagement
The article's framing model treats contextual factors as time-invariant and therefore excludes them from the longitudinal model
target_learners: higher education students in online/blended programs
target_learning_goals: understanding longitudinal student engagement and achievement trajectories for monitoring and support
examples: The method was applied to 106 students over 15 courses of a problem-based learning healthcare program, yielding three trajectory clusters: Engaged high-achieving starters, Average starters, and Disengaged starters
key_sources: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas, Satu Helske, Stefan Hrastinski. (2023). The longitudinal association between engagement and achievement varies by time, students' profiles, and achievement state: A full program study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104787

article_title: Local Potential Integrated Science Video to Improve SPS and Concept Mastery
citation: Wilujeng, I., Suryadarma, I. G. P., Ertika, & Dwandaru, W. S. B. (2020). Local Potential Integrated Science Video to Improve SPS and Concept Mastery. International Journal of Instruction, 13(4), 197-214. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13413a
title: Expert-validated science learning video integrating the Wukirsari Village MHP plant, released on YouTube
description: An educational natural science video developed in this research and validated by experts, integrating energy concepts with a local micro-hydro power plant in Wukirsari Village, Bantul. It "contains experimental activities that give examples of learning procedures so that students can easily understand the learning material and turn their knowledge into practice." It was uploaded to YouTube to reach a wider audience and can be searched under the channel Ertika.PLTMH.
requirements: Requires the ability to see and hear at the same time, as video is categorized as a medium providing audio-visual information on concepts, principles, procedures, and applications
constraints: The article notes a lack of hands-on approach to the MHP plant topic compared to directly visiting the plant
target_learning_goals: concept mastery of energy in systems of life
examples: Students in the experimental class watched the video during learning activities and followed procedural steps they could directly see and listen to throughout the video
key_sources: Wilujeng, I., Suryadarma, I. G. P., Ertika, & Dwandaru, W. S. B. (2020). Local Potential Integrated Science Video to Improve SPS and Concept Mastery. International Journal of Instruction, 13(4), 197-214. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13413a

article_title: Team-Based Learning in the Meta Horizon Workroom: A Pilot Study on Its Potential Effectiveness for Pharmacology Teaching.
citation: Khaiyam Abdullah, Battersby Lucy, Porter Ellie, de Oliveira Ana Correia, Sadiq Soban. (2025). Team‐Based Learning in the Meta Horizon Workroom: A Pilot Study on Its Potential Effectiveness for Pharmacology Teaching. Pharmacology Research & Perspectives. https://doi.org/10.1002/prp2.70170
title: Meta Horizon Workroom team-based learning session for pharmacology (60-minute virtual application exercise)
description: A virtual TBL session delivered in the Meta Horizon Workroom with Meta Quest 2 headsets, in which students created avatars and collaborated on a pharmacology case scenario about hypertension and its treatment. The article states: "The TBL session lasted for approximately 60 min, comprising a 10‐min introduction and VR headset training, a 40‐min application exercise and discussion, and a 10‐min post‐session questionnaire." Faculty members were present in the session to facilitate discussion and give immediate feedback, and interactive tools included 3D models and shared whiteboards.
requirements: Meta Quest 2 VR headsets and access to the Meta Horizon Workroom platform
Faculty members present within the MHW session to facilitate discussions and provide immediate feedback
Individual preparatory reading of assigned materials before the session
Initial VR headset and MHW training for participants
constraints: Piloted with seven questionnaire respondents from a cohort of approximately 82 students
Participants were recruited for prior pharmacology competence and comfort with immersive technology
Technical issues such as echo and login difficulties occurred during the session
target_learning_goals: Applying pharmacology concepts (hypertension and its treatment) to a clinical case scenario
Collaboration and communication within team-based learning
examples: Students created avatars in MHW and discussed a hypertension-focused pharmacology case scenario; the cybersickness questionnaire showed no concerns pre and post exposure.
key_sources: Khaiyam Abdullah, Battersby Lucy, Porter Ellie, de Oliveira Ana Correia, Sadiq Soban. (2025). Team‐Based Learning in the Meta Horizon Workroom: A Pilot Study on Its Potential Effectiveness for Pharmacology Teaching. Pharmacology Research & Perspectives. https://doi.org/10.1002/prp2.70170

article_title: Examining interviewer bias in medical school admissions: The interplay between applicant and interviewer gender and its effects on interview outcomes.
citation: Tsikas Stefanos A., Dauer Karina. (2024). Examining interviewer bias in medical school admissions: The interplay between applicant and interviewer gender and its effects on interview outcomes. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0309293
title: MHH semi-structured selection interview procedure with weighted total score (49% interview, 51% Abitur)
description: The Hannover Medical School selection procedure ranked applicants on a weighted Total score from 0 to 15 points, calculated as 0.49 × Interview grade + 0.51 × Abitur grade, with the Abitur dominant by legal requirement. Two-physician committees evaluated four categories (personal qualifications, professional aspects, extracurricular activities, and a subjective overall impression), each weighted 25% of the interview grade, on a 0–15 scale, agreeing on a common score. Interviews targeted qualities "only inadequately reflected in high school grades or aptitude tests" and lasted at least 20 but no longer than 30 minutes.
requirements: Committees of two MHH faculty physicians from different sections, with at least one clinically active doctor
A pre-interview questionnaire providing interviewers information on school subjects, hobbies, vocational training or experiences as foreign exchange students
constraints: The interviews were not standardized, meaning that no uniform questions were asked to all candidates
Committee-level common scoring means potential interviewer bias can only be investigated at the commission level, not at the individual level
target_learners: medical school applicants preselected on high school grades
target_learning_goals: assessment of social competence, societal engagement, motivation to study, and self-reflection
examples: From 2006 to 2019, approximately 400 applicants per year were invited, on average 370 interviews per year were included in the data, and around 150 applicants were admitted annually.
key_sources: Tsikas Stefanos A., Dauer Karina. (2024). Examining interviewer bias in medical school admissions: The interplay between applicant and interviewer gender and its effects on interview outcomes. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0309293

article_title: Clinical experience can compensate for inferior academic achievements in an undergraduate objective structured clinical examination.
citation: Tsikas, Stefanos A.; Afshar, Kambiz. (2023). Clinical experience can compensate for inferior academic achievements in an undergraduate objective structured clinical examination. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04082-x
title: The Hannover Medical School (MHH) OSCE in the module 'Diagnostic Methods'
description: The MHH OSCE is the final examination of the second-year module 'Diagnostic Methods', taken at the end of the second academic year en route to M1. It is "a course of nine stations" covering internal medicine and neurological examination (125 points), structured X-ray diagnosis (25 points), two practical skills stations such as blood collection and intramuscular injection (50 points), and a medical consultation with anamnesis and diagnosis delivered to a standardised patient (100 points). Sixty percent of points are needed to pass; underperformance in one station can be compensated by good results elsewhere.
requirements: Stations worth 25 points are completed in seven minutes and 50-point stations in 15 minutes, within a 95-minute course including changeover time.
constraints: Contents and timing of the OSCE are specific to the MHH and its curriculum; the authors state results cannot be generalized to other sites.
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in their second year
target_learning_goals: Practical clinical skills, diagnostic competence, and doctor-patient communication
examples: Students reach almost 90% of the possible 50 points at the medical-skills stations, the easiest part of the exam in the sample.
key_sources: Tsikas, Stefanos A.; Afshar, Kambiz. (2023). Clinical experience can compensate for inferior academic achievements in an undergraduate objective structured clinical examination. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04082-x

article_title: A pilot randomised controlled study of the mental health first aid eLearning course with UK medical students.
citation: Davies E. Bethan, Beever Emmeline, Glazebrook Cris. (2018). A pilot randomised controlled study of the mental health first aid eLearning course with UK medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1154-x
title: The MHFA eLearning course: six self-paced modules teaching the ALGEE action plan
description: The MHFA eLearning course is a structured online programme teaching mental health literacy and first aid skills. It "comprises six modules completed consecutively", covering depression, anxiety, eating disorders, psychosis and substance use problems, each with a disorder-specific action plan. "Content is delivered through text, images, audio, videos and interactive activities, and completed at the user's own pace over approximately 6–8 h." Central to MHFA is the five-step ALGEE action plan: approach the person, assess and assist with any crisis; listen non-judgementally; give support and information; encourage appropriate professional help; and encourage other support strategies. Participants also received the MHFA Manual and a supplementary medical students' booklet.
requirements: Regular access to the internet and a laptop/computer
Approximately 6–8 h of self-paced study time
constraints: In this study some participants took longer than the estimated 6–8 h, and some mentioned difficulties in rehearsing new skills through eLearning
target_learners: UK undergraduate and graduate-entry medical students in their first to third year
target_learning_goals: Improve mental health literacy and knowledge of specific mental disorders
Improve quality of mental health first aid intentions and confidence to help someone with a mental health problem
examples: In the pilot RCT, 20 of 27 intervention participants registered an account; 11 completed all six modules, and feedback was generally positive, with ten stating they would recommend the course to fellow medical students
key_sources: Davies E. Bethan, Beever Emmeline, Glazebrook Cris. (2018). A pilot randomised controlled study of the mental health first aid eLearning course with UK medical students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1154-x
